notes.meaning: Jesus saw that his friends were upset. They had just heard about a traitor, about Peter's coming denial, and that Jesus was leaving. He tells them not to let fear shake them, but to trust him just as they trust God. That is a bold claim: Jesus asks for the same trust we give to God himself.

Jesus pictures heaven as his Father's home. "Many rooms" means there is plenty of space for all his people, and a place for each one. If this hope were false, he would have told them plainly. His going away, through his death, rising and return to heaven, is how he gets the place ready for them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars link the word for "rooms" to a traveller's rest stop, and the early writer Origen saw it as stages on the road to God. Others prefer "lasting home" and suggest the dwelling place may finally be "in" Jesus himself.

notes.meaning: Jesus promises to come back and take his people to be with him. This points first to his second coming at the end of time. Many also take comfort from it for each believer at death. Best of all, heaven means being where Jesus is.
Jesus tells them they already know where he is going and how to get there. He was going to the Father. The way is Jesus himself. They knew more than they thought they did.

Thomas honestly admits he is confused. The disciples still pictured an earthly kingdom, so they thought Jesus meant some place on a map. His honest question opens the door to one of Jesus' greatest answers.

Jesus does not just show the way to God. He is the way. He is the truth, fully reliable and the real thing the Old Testament pictures pointed to. He is the life who makes people alive to God, and no one comes to God as Father except through him and his death for us. Being sincere is not enough without him.

Jesus gently scolds them. If they had really known him, they would know the Father too, because Jesus shows us exactly what God is like. From now on, he says, they do know God and have seen him, in Jesus.
Philip asks for a visible sight of God, like Moses once asked for. He thinks that would settle every question. But he has missed what Jesus just said.
Jesus is saddened. After more than three years together, Philip still does not see who he is. Whoever has seen Jesus has seen the Father. Jesus' holiness, kindness and power show us God's own heart.

Jesus and the Father are joined in a way no two others ever are. Jesus' words are not just his own ideas; they come from the Father. His works are the Father at work in him. Both his teaching and his deeds show God's greatness.
Jesus asks them to take him at his word. If they find that hard, they should at least look at his works. His miracles showed God's power and backed up what he said.

Jesus promises that those who believe in him will carry on his work. They will even do "greater" works, because he is going to the Father and will send the Holy Spirit. The traditional reading takes "greater" to mean bigger in reach and number, not more amazing. Jesus worked in one small land, but the apostles took the good news to many nations, and thousands turned to God in a single day.

differ.view: The works are greater because they happen in the age of the Spirit, after the cross, and they include no less than miracles and healings.
The greater works are mainly the spread of the gospel and many conversions, not believers doing more spectacular miracles than Jesus.

notes.meaning: Jesus gives a wide promise about prayer. To ask "in his name" means to come trusting what he has done for us, not our own goodness, and to want what God wants. It is not a magic phrase added at the end. He answers so that the Father is honored through the Son, and verse 14 even invites us to pray to Jesus himself.
Jesus says the true sign of love for him is doing what he says. Tears at his leaving were not enough. Love is the root, and obedience is the fruit.

Jesus will ask the Father to send "another Advocate," a helper of the same kind as Jesus. The word means someone who stands by your side: a helper, comforter and one who speaks up for you. This is the Holy Spirit, who teaches the truth and, unlike Jesus in the flesh, will stay forever. People who live only for this world cannot see or welcome him, but believers know him, and he will live inside them.

Jesus will not leave them like children with no parent. "I will come to you," he says. He came back to them when he rose from the dead, he comes to them by his Spirit, and he will come again at the end.

Soon the world will not see him, because he will die. But his followers will see him, alive after he rises, and by faith after that. Because Jesus lives, they will live too: a new life with God now, and resurrection life forever.

"That day" points to the time after Jesus rose and the Spirit came. Then they will understand how closely Jesus is joined to the Father. They will also understand that Jesus is in them and they are in him, a bond nothing can break.

Again, love for Jesus shows in keeping his commands. Those who love him are loved by the Father and by Jesus. This does not mean our love comes first, because God loved us first. It means they will sense his love more and more, and Jesus will make himself known to them in a deeper, spiritual way.

Another disciple named Judas, also called Thaddaeus, asks a question. John makes clear he is not the traitor. Judas likely expected Jesus to show himself to the whole world as a king, so he wonders why only to them.

Jesus repeats that love shows itself in obedience. Then he makes an amazing promise. The Father and the Son will come and make their home with the one who loves him. This is not a short visit but a lasting stay, here and now.
The opposite is also true. Whoever does not love Jesus will not keep his words. And his words can be trusted, because they come from the Father who sent him.
Jesus has said all this while still with them in person, and he stands by every word. Even if they do not grasp it all yet, his teaching is like a seed that will grow later.

The Holy Spirit, sent by the Father as Jesus' representative, will be their teacher. He will help them remember and understand what Jesus said, which guided the apostles as they preached and wrote. He would not bring a new gospel, but make Jesus' words clear. He still helps believers today remember what they have learned.

"Peace" was a normal goodbye, but Jesus means much more. He leaves them his own peace: peace with God and calm in the heart. The world's wishes are often empty and its peace does not last, but his is real and lasting. So they need not be troubled or afraid.

Jesus reminds them he is going away and coming back. If they loved him rightly, they would be glad he was going home to the Father. "The Father is greater than I" does not mean Jesus is less than fully God, for he also said he and the Father are one. It speaks of Jesus as the one sent, in his humble state on earth, about to enter great glory.

differ.view: The Father is greater than Jesus as a man; as God, neither is greater or less than the other.
Jesus is not comparing natures at all, but his humbled role as the go-between who leads us to God with the heavenly glory he was about to enter.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine taught that Jesus is less than the Father only in his human servant form and equal in his divine nature. Catholic Answers adds that the Father has higher rank as Father and as the one who sent Jesus, without denying Jesus is God.

notes.meaning: Jesus tells them ahead of time about his death, rising and return to the Father. When it happens, they will remember his words. Then their faith will grow, because they will see he knew it all beforehand and that it was God's plan.
Time is short, so Jesus will not say much more. "The prince of this world" is Satan, coming for a final attack. But Satan has no claim on Jesus. There is no sin in him for Satan to grab hold of.

Jesus is not dragged to the cross. He goes willingly, because it is the Father's plan, so the world will see how much he loves the Father. Then he says, "Get up! Let us go," calling his friends to follow as he walks toward his suffering. Many think they left the room here and he kept talking on the way.
